accuracy.reason: All eight objectives are accurate with explicit scope: response reuse, origin-relative freshness, conditional validation, storage/privacy policy, variant matching, versioning/purge, bounded stale allowances and layer-specific measurement. Primary sources support critical claims; no universal cookie bypass, instant purge or availability guarantee.

evidence.quote: Age estimates seconds since generation or successful validation at origin, including time spent through caches. If this response arrives with Age: 90, ignoring transit and clock differences, the browser is 30 seconds past its lifetime. The CDN has 300 − 90 = 210 seconds of freshness left. Receiving it does not start a new full lifetime.

A shared response reused for the wrong user can leak private data. Cookie and Set-Cookie do not automatically create per-user cache entries or universally prevent caching. Authorization-bearing requests have special shared-cache restrictions, but response policy can permit reuse; authentication alone is no universal CDN bypass guarantee.

mechanisms.reason: Teaches request/response state transitions, independent browser/shared lifetimes, stale-body retention, validator branches and variant selection. Both diagrams correctly show where a hit stops work and how a 304 retains a body while a 200 can replace it. Every card mechanism supports the actual learner explanation.

evidence.quote: If unchanged, origin returns 304 Not Modified without a replacement body. The CDN updates applicable stored metadata, including freshness information, and uses its retained body to answer the browser's ordinary GET.

At age 75 it is 15 seconds stale: the additional 30-second background-validation window permits reuse while refreshing, through age 90. At age 150 with an eligible error, it is 90 seconds stale: the error allowance lasts another 120 seconds after expiry, through age 180. At age 200 neither extension still permits stale reuse.

coherence.reason: Definitions precede freshness and validation, then storage permission and key correctness, deployment, failure behavior and measurement. Browser/CDN/origin distinctions persist across both diagrams and every objective; caching policy is consistently separate from authorization.

evidence.quote: An HTTP cache stores response bodies and metadata, such as status and headers, for reuse. A browser private cache serves that user agent. A content delivery network (CDN) runs shared caches at edge servers near users. The origin is the server responsible for the resource.

Purging CDN entries does not evict fresh browser copies or erase downloaded content. Unpublishing can stop future origin access and trigger purges, but already delivered public content cannot be instantly revoked. Choose cache lifetimes with that limit in mind before publishing.

decisions.reason: Gives causal criteria for public/private/sensitive policy, variant preservation or bypass, immutable versus mutable deployment, bounded stale tolerance and omitting shared caching when costs exceed reuse. The learner transfers these choices with their limits rather than relying on prior knowledge.

evidence.quote: Irrelevant tracking parameters can create extra entries and fewer hits. Exclude them only after confirming they do not change the response. Vary does not change the URL, grant permission or override private/no-store. Correctly separated public variants are not permission to share private responses.

For a low-traffic application serving mostly private or rarely reused responses, omit shared caching if measured benefits do not justify those costs. Compare reuse, latency and total cost. Keep privacy rules intact rather than making private content shared to improve a metric.

clarity.reason: Defines technical terms before use and makes timing arithmetic and two validation outcomes explicit. All actual learner quotes match slide text and entail the associated answers. The diagrams label cache boundaries and response outcomes without implying fresh retention, database synchronization or revocation.

evidence.quote: Cache-Control is a response header carrying caching rules called directives. A fresh response is young enough for reuse without validation under its policy. A stale response has reached its freshness limit; its body need not be deleted. Freshness is permission to reuse, not proof that origin content is unchanged.
304 saves retransmitting the body across the validation hop. Origin was still contacted and may run application logic or query a database to decide whether the representation changed.

outcomes.reason: Actual learner distinguishes cached HTTP bodies/metadata from database replicas, names browser/CDN/origin, traces cold response return and both hit paths. It computes 800/1000=80% and conditional 200 origin requests, excludes browser hits and byte/work inference, and weighs public reuse and latency against charges and operational costs for the private low-traffic case. The cited slides entail each conclusion.

It sends preserved v1 in If-None-Match, distinguishes 304 metadata update/retained body from cacheable 200 replacement, and identifies continuing origin/application work. All requested mechanisms are explicitly taught and quoted.

Quotes support each choice without inventing a universal bypass.

It removes tracking inputs only after proving irrelevance and explicitly rejects Vary as permission or an override of private/no-store. This meets all five criteria with cited mechanisms.

It selects mutable-page freshness/validation, checks provider purge URL/variant/layer coverage and completion, and denies recall of browser/downloaded copies on unpublish. All four criteria are supported; no instantaneous propagation claim.

sourceChecks.claim: Checked CDN definition, distributed nearby shared servers and origin-offload benefit. RFC9111 additionally establishes stored responses and private/shared reuse; the two hit paths follow those boundaries, not database replication.

MDN explicitly distinguishes max-age and shared-only s-maxage and deducts Age from freshness. RFC9111 confirms fresh/stale calculation and non-guaranteed retention. The 60/300/Age90 arithmetic and reuse-versus-content-change distinction are sound.

MDN documents opaque ETags and matching If-None-Match producing bodyless 304. RFC9111 section4.3.4 supports updating stored metadata and retaining a body; changed 200 replacement is policy-qualified. A network validation need not eliminate origin application work.

RFC9111 confirms unqualified no-cache validation, private prohibition on shared storage, no-store obligations, conditional Authorization reuse and that Set-Cookie does not inhibit caching. RFC6265 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6265.html) confirms Set-Cookie/Cookie state flow. The privacy choices and origin authorization are correctly separated.

Cloudflare key docs confirm full URL/query defaults, query exclusion options and header matching. Supplemental https://developers.cloudflare.com/cache/concepts/vary/ explicitly documents configured Vary actions and Accept-Language matching/normalization. The lesson requires verification rather than promising universal provider support; irrelevant-input fragmentation follows key distinctions.

Cloudflare purge docs describe targeting and distinguish accepted requests from verified cache eviction. https://developers.cloudflare.com/cache/how-to/edge-browser-cache-ttl/ explicitly says purge does not affect visitor browser assets. MDN Cache-Control supports versioned immutable assets. Parent-reference, mutable-page and delivered-copy limits follow these separate cache states.

RFC5861 defines bounded stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error relative to freshness expiry, with background validation and eligible errors. The 60+30=90 and 60+120=180 windows, age75/150/200 cases, support and retained-copy assumptions are correct, without an availability guarantee.

Cloudflare hit-ratio source defines hits over requests and cautions that this is not the complete performance picture. The 80%/200 example explicitly supplies the extra assumptions; byte, browser and background-work distinctions are sound. AWS primary FAQ https://aws.amazon.com/cloudfront/faqs/ confirms requests and transfer can be charged; no price or guaranteed savings is claimed.
